Results were powered by equities trading, which exceeded revenue expectations by $909 million. In this article MS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:46 04:46 Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick: 'I'm cautiously optimistic about the fourth quarter' Squawk on the Street Morgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise. Here's what the company reported: Earnings per share: $3.03 vs. $2.91 LSEG estimate Revenue: $20.34 billion vs. $19.95 billion LSEG estimate The company said profit climbed 6.5% to $4.91 billion, or $3.03 a share. Revenue climbed 12% to $20.34 billion. The firm's equities trading division, long a marquee business for Morgan Stanley, posted a 41% increase in revenue to $5.8 billion, exceeding the StreetAccount estimate by about $909 million. Morgan Stanley cited widespread strength across its equities products and regions, but cited Asia as a source of particular strength in the quarter. The gains in that business helped offset disappointments elsewhere. Fixed income trading revenue fell 7% to $2.01 billion, driven by declines in credit and commodities, which is roughly $260 million below expectations. Investment banking revenue edged 2% higher to $2.16 billion, about $110 million below expectations. The bank cited an increase in advisory revenue on more completed mergers, but declines in equity underwriting on lower IPOs and a decline in fixed income underwriting. Still, the results were "good, but not great," as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Wednesday in a note. Morgan Stanley shares declined about 3% in midday trading. The economy is subject to two key forces right now: the boost from the AI buildout and the drag from geopolitical strife, Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick told CNBC's Leslie Picker on Wednesday. Starting in early September, concerns with overseas conflict, inflation and surging yields slowed activity across Wall Street, Pick noted. "The interaction of the AI phenomenon and geopolitics has been the dominant reality the whole year," Pick said. "It's really two very different stories, and I'd like to think that we are going to have the first narrative, the positive narrative, if we can get some control over the geopolitics." Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Netflix said on Wednesday it will lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, according to a memo obtained by CNBC. The job cuts will largely impact the product, tech, legal and HR teams. "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources," Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the email to employees. "Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We'll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. "Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors," the note said. Netflix said it did not have additional comments beyond the co-CEOs' memo. The company is due to report quarterly earnings on Oct. 20. The layoffs come just a few weeks after Sarandos told attendees at the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company was "not growing as fast as I want." Netflix has faced a paradox in recent months. It continues to post solid profits and remains the biggest player in the streaming realm, but its viewing time has stagnated and the main driver of new subscriber acquisitions has been its password-sharing crackdown and the launch of a cheaper, ad-supported tier. Netflix's biggest threat has been YouTube, but looming on the horizon is Skydance . The combined entity of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery has plans to integrate the two companies' streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max. Netflix has diversified its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. At the same time, it's lacked the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriber growth and viewership. And Netflix is not the only company looking to cut costs in the media space. Last month, Disney said it would lay off around 300 employees , with the majority of cuts coming from human resources and technology roles. — CNBC's Julia Boorstin and Stephen Desaulniers contributed to this report. Revenue was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading. Misses in fixed income and equities trading revenue totaled roughly $750 million. In this article BAC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 5:33 05:33 Bank of America CEO on $1.2 billion fine: We're on the right course to remediate everything Squawk on the Street Bank of America on Wednesday posted a sharp profit decline after being hit with a $1.2 billion penalty by U.S. regulators, while revenue also disappointed after trading operations generated about $750 million less than expected. Shares of the bank fell as much as 8% in morning trading. Here's what the company reported: Earnings per share: 91 cents, may not compare with $1.10 expected by LSEG Revenue: $30.12 billion vs. $30.69 billion expected by LSEG The bank's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Excluding the penalty, which sapped income by 17 cents, EPS would've been $1.08 a share. Companywide revenue rose 3.2% to $30.12 billion in the quarter, on an FTE basis, but that was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading operations. Fixed income trading revenue fell 17% to $2.55 billion on weakness in mortgages, municipals and credit activity. That is roughly $450 million below the StreetAccount estimate. Equities trading revenue climbed 10% to $2.51 billion, but that was also below analysts' expectations, by nearly $300 million. The trading disappointment comes after CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts last month that trading revenue would be roughly flat; instead the combined bond and stock trading results fell by 5%. Investment banking revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion, roughly in line with expectations and Moynihan's September guidance. Net interest income, a key profitability driver watched closely by Bank of America investors, rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion, slightly edging out the $16.53 billion StreetAccount estimate. 'Worst in class' In a research note published Wednesday, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo called the firm's capital markets results "easily worst in class" for the quarter. The Treasury episode, in which U.S. regulators said the company failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions, sparked questions as to whether Moynihan has a handle on controls at the second-biggest U.S. bank by assets. On the company's earnings call Wednesday, several analysts remarked on the sharp decline in Bank of America shares and pressed Moynihan about earlier guidance that compliance costs would be contained. "Clearly you've had a huge charge this morning," JPMorgan analyst Vivek Juneja said. "It's not that you can't absorb a billion … But obviously it's a reputational and confidence issue." Other analysts questioned management on the pace of future share repurchases and asked about the bank's underperformance in trading. Management blamed the firm's bond trading results on the sharp rise in interest rates during the period. "It just happens when rates go up 85 basis points in a quarter, that tends not to be good for" credit and mortgage trading businesses, CFO Alastair Borthwick said. 'The right course' Later Wednesday in an interview with CNBC's Leslie Picker , Moynihan didn't commit to a timeline on the resolution of regulatory issues. "We got to do the work, and then the regulators look at it," Moynihan said. "So I don't want to speculate about the precise timeline." The CEO added that he was "confident that we are on the right course to remediate everything." Moynihan took the helm in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure making amends for mortgage-related abuses in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. The Treasury fine, announced on Tuesday, added 11th-hour intrigue to what was an otherwise fairly routine bank earnings week. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo posted mixed results, with JPMorgan missing EPS and revenue estimates for the first time in years. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Shares of Bending Spoons skyrocketed 35% after a new securities filing revealed that Berkshire Hathaway made a fresh $330 million investment into the company. The latest infusion follows the conglomerate's $600 million investment from July, when the Italy-based serial acquirer went public on the Nasdaq. Under the deal, Bending Spoons will issue 10 million ordinary shares to Berkshire at $33 a share. "Bending Spoons continuously evaluates M&A opportunities, and our pipeline remains strong," said Francesco Patarnello, Bending Spoons' co-founder and head of business acquisitions, in a statement. "We believe Berkshire Hathaway's investment reflects confidence in our team and Platform and will further enhance our financial flexibility and ability to pursue attractive acquisitions as part of our broader financing strategy." The investment now brings Berkshire's stake in the company to 4%, according to the filing, and is the conglomerate's latest investment decision as CEO Greg Abel took the helm from founder and legendary investor Warren Buffett at the start of the year.
